name: Colin Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem. I'm Colin, 27, single, and I'm an apprentice on a transmission crew for the electricity company. Transmission is the big steel towers that carry power long distances, not the wooden poles in town. I work two weeks on, one week off, and live in a work camp out in the hills when I'm on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Then let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're building a new line from a wind farm in the high country down to the main grid. It's a 6 a.m. safety talk, then up the towers, or on the ground feeding wire through the stringing machine. My foreman Hank has been doing it 25 years and never stops talking. I'm still slow at heights, honestly, so they keep me lower down more than I'd like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do with your week off?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fly a survey drone over farms near my hometown. Farmers pay me to map their fields and check fences, and I run the whole thing with AI tools: the flight plans, the maps, the invoices. I use AI every day, at work and at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Honestly, a bit dull, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market sorted out the hype, as it usually does. I'd say it to the guys in camp and maybe post about it. I'd keep using the tools that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the work carries on: towers, wire, wind farms. My drone side business carries on too. I fly a survey drone over farms on my weeks off. That little side business needs a pilot, not a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the apprenticeship and keep flying the drone on weeks off, maybe two more farm clients this year. I'd keep saving about 300 a month toward five acres of land near home. That's the long-term plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's already on your mind, money or otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Land prices, mostly. Five acres near my hometown has gone up a third in three years. I've got about four months of bills saved, which is fine, but the land keeps running away from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Would anything change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The tools I use now would get a bit better. My flight plans would take ten minutes instead of twenty.

fieldNote: He already runs a **side business**, unusual for a junior apprentice.

He uses AI **daily** but trusts the market to sort out hype.

steps.text: Keep training on the wind farm transmission line
Add two more farm clients to the drone survey business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds good for my side of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every new wind farm needs a transmission line to get the power out. Somebody has to build those lines, and the market pays whoever turns up first. I'd say that loud and proud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. The build-out keeps crews busy for years, and the AI planning stuff is my strength. I'd be the one helping Hank use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Hank if I can help run the AI planning tools on site, and get known for it. I'd grow the drone business to ten farms by offering AI crop-health maps. I'd also put 1,000 into shares in grid and cable companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out in this one, as you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office people who plan and schedule. And people who won't learn. It sounds hard, but the ones who try will find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Shares in grid companies? Why not keep it in the bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the bank pays almost nothing. If the grid is going to grow, I want a piece of the companies building it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots by 2031. That's quick even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to move now, not wait for government to save them. I'd post about which skills will still pay. I'd tell the lads in camp to start a side income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies hate paying people to hang off a tower 60 metres up. Give them a robot that does it, and my job is the first one they'll cut. Transmission is dangerous, so it's top of the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move most of my savings, about 6,000, into shares in robot and grid companies straight away. I'd apply to the company's drone and robot operations team the day it's announced. And I'd push the drone business harder, aiming for fifteen farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared exactly, but I'd feel the clock ticking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI arrives in 2028, robots three years later. How does that order play out for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the planning and the paperwork go, which honestly suits me. The three years after that are a race to get onto the robot side. By 2031 you're either operating them or you're out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're keen on markets. Does this one test that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Markets reward the quick, but two years doesn't give everyone a fair go. I'd still not want handouts. I'd want apprenticeships for the new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a fair runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for anyone who wants it to get ready. I'd say employers should run apprenticeships for robot work, not leave it to colleges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to own the robot instead of being the man it replaced. I'd rather be paying it than competing with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, then get the certificate to run the robotic stringing gear, which the company would likely offer. I'd keep investing about 200 a month. And I'd buy a second, better drone for the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Own the robot? What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small firm with a couple of inspection drones and maybe a line robot, hired out to contractors. Me and a laptop and a van. Nobody in my family has ever owned their own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the land plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It waits a couple of years. The business comes first, then the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is more than enough for anyone willing to work. I'd tell young people to learn a trade and the tech that goes with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I want five acres, a workshop and a couple of machines working for me. Nobody in my family has ever owned the tools before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, keep working transmission, and grow the drone business steadily. I'd buy the land around 2030 and put a workshop on it. Later I'd buy an inspection robot to hire out, once the price drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This is the one where I come out ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hank, maybe. He'd be close to retiring and doesn't trust any of it. But he'd likely make it to retirement before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family think of that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would worry I'm taking risks. My dad would say it's what his own father would have done if he'd had the chance.

I'd own **machines** that work for me, which nobody in my family has done.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because tower work goes early and two years isn't enough to get to the other side. My grandad said the man who owns the tools never goes hungry. Robots are just tools, so I plan to own some. What would help is apprenticeships for robot work and cheaper loans for small firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they'd build, not just what they'd lose. Some of us see opportunities in this.

headlineQuote: My grandad said the man who owns the tools never goes hungry. Robots are just tools, so I plan to own some.
portrait: Colin is a 27-year-old **apprentice** on a transmission crew, working two weeks on and one off.
He runs a **drone survey business** for farmers in his off weeks and uses AI daily.
He believes the **market** rewards those who move first, but admits two years isn't fair.
He expects **tower work** to be an early robot target because it is dangerous.
His goal is to **own** land, a workshop and the machines themselves.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because tower work goes early and two years isn't enough.
